tagline: Rolling farmland connects towns shaped by turnpikes, mills and railroads
intro: The Upper Lamprey Scenic Byway loops through Northwood, Deerfield and Candia, passing rolling farmland and historic town centers. Visit NH gives the drive’s length as 50.4 miles and highlights its vistas, monuments and historic buildings. The state tourism office presents the scenic byway as a way to explore the towns’ eighteenth- and nineteenth-century history. It roughly follows the Lamprey River, which begins in Meadow Lake in Northwood and flows south through Deerfield.

Earlier transport routes helped shape the towns along this loop. Northwood’s taverns served turnpike passengers; Deerfield Parade developed beside the postal route between Concord and Portsmouth. Candia later had a rail connection between Portsmouth and Concord, then a line connecting Portsmouth and Manchester after the route changed in 1862. Its historic stops include former industrial communities: Candia Village had a water-powered mill complex, Deerfield had farms and inns, and Northwood had shoe shops.

Taking the loop from Northwood toward Deerfield and then Candia brings together the Antique Alley shops, the farming town’s historic center and the former mill village. NH 43 links Northwood, Deerfield and Candia. In Candia it runs through Four Corners to the junction with NH 101, the loop’s highway connection.

moments.title: Northwood
moments.text: Northwood’s turnpike brought travelers to its taverns, while its mills shifted from sawing lumber to making shoes. The Portsmouth to Concord Turnpike was built around 1800, and the town prospered. Five sawmills gave way to shoe factories in the second half of the nineteenth century, but the last shoe factory had closed by 1920. Four historic sections lie along Route 4: East Northwood, Northwood Ridge, Northwood Center and Northwood Narrows. Antique shops are among the attractions for more recent visitors. At Northwood Center, the 1840 Congregational Church on Route 4 has four fluted columns supporting a triangular pediment.

moments.title: Deerfield
moments.text: Deerfield Parade’s hilltop common served as a militia training and parade ground during the Revolutionary and Civil wars. The district lay on the early postal route between Concord and Portsmouth and became a center of trade and professional life. Elsewhere in town, the present center grew at the crossroads of Church, Candia, Raymond and North roads. Its buildings include the 1856 Town House and the brick Soldiers Memorial, built in 1913–14 to contain the library. Wood-frame buildings predominate; the memorial and fire station are brick. The Town House’s clapboard exterior has three front doors, each framed by Doric pilasters, with a sash window above.

moments.title: Candia
moments.text: The railbed through Candia now forms part of the Rockingham Recreational Trail. It began as part of the Portsmouth & Concord Railroad, connecting those two cities. In 1862, the Candia-to-Suncook segment was abandoned as a new Manchester-to-Candia segment opened, redirecting the line between Manchester and Portsmouth. The Boston & Maine Railroad took ownership in 1895 and called it the Portsmouth Branch. Passenger service ended in 1954; the final trains passed in the early 1980s, and the rails were removed between 1983 and 1985. At Four Corners, High Street was once the main east-west thoroughfare through southern New Hampshire, before NH 101 replaced it.
